claim: Morphogen gradients can instruct cells about their position in a patterned tissue.
source: Morphogen gradients can instruct cells about their position in a patterned tissue.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus in developmental biology.

claim: Non-linear morphogen decay has been suggested to increase gradient precision by reducing the sensitivity to variability in the morphogen source.
source: Non-linear morphogen decay has been suggested to increase gradient precision by reducing the sensitivity to variability in the morphogen source.
evidence: This statement references prior theoretical work, implicitly citing previous literature.

claim: Non-linear decay reduces the positional error close to the source.
source: While we confirm that non-linear decay reduces the positional error close to the source, the reduction is very small for physiological noise levels.
evidence: This is supported by the cell-based simulations presented in the manuscript, as shown in multiple figures.

claim: The reduction in positional error from non-linear decay is very small for physiological noise levels.
source: While we confirm that non-linear decay reduces the positional error close to the source, the reduction is very small for physiological noise levels.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Far from the source, the positional error is much larger for non-linear decay in tissues that pose a flux barrier to the morphogen at the boundary.
source: Far from the source, the positional error is much larger for non-linear decay in tissues that pose a flux barrier to the morphogen at the boundary.
evidence: This is a key finding from the simulations shown in the manuscript.

claim: A physiological role of morphogen decay dynamics in patterning precision appears unlikely.
source: In light of this new data, a physiological role of morphogen decay dynamics in patterning precision appears unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Readout positions mark the boundary locations between domains of different cell fates.
source: Thus, these readout positions mark the boundary locations between domains of different cell fates.
evidence: This is an inference from the French flag model described in the text.

claim: Variations in the morphogen profile result in variations in the readout positions.
source: Variations in the morphogen profile result in variations in the readout positions.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the French flag model and the definition of readout positions.

claim: The accuracy of the spatial information carried by morphogen gradients can be quantified with the positional error, defined as the standard deviation of the readout positions over different gradient realizations.
source: The accuracy of the spatial information carried by morphogen gradients can be quantified with the positional error, which is defined as the standard deviation of the readout positions over different gradient realizations (Vetter and Iber, 2022):
evidence: This definition is cited from Vetter and Iber, 2022.

claim: Morphogen dynamics are often described by reaction-diffusion equations of a specific form.
source: Morphogen dynamics are often described by reaction-diffusion equations of the form (Lander et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement cites Lander et al., 2009 and describes a common modeling approach.

claim: Linear decay leads to exponential gradient profiles.
source: Linear decay leads to exponential gradient profiles (Figure 1B) of the form (Lander et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lander et al., 2002 and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Non-linear decay results in shifted power-law gradients.
source: Non-linear decay, on the other hand, results in shifted power-law gradients (Figure 1C; Eldar et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eldar et al., 2003 and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Non-linear decay would arise in case of cell lineage transport, when ligands interact with receptor clusters, or if ligand binding results in receptor upregulation.
source: Non-linear decay would for instance arise in case of cell lineage transport, when ligands interact with receptor clusters, or if ligand binding results in receptor upregulation, as is the case for several morphogens, most prominently for Hedgehog (Hh) (Eldar et al., 2003; Nahmad and Stathopoulos, 2009; Wartlick et al., 2009; Balaskas et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing mechanisms that lead to non-linear decay.

claim: Embryos are subject to molecular noise, which can cause fluctuations in morphogen production and transport rates.
source: Embryos are subject to molecular noise, which can cause fluctuations in morphogen production and transport rates, and consequently, in the gradient amplitudes and morphogen fluxes from the source to the patterned cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about biological systems.

claim: In the case of linear decay, the shift is only related to the relative morphogen influx or amplitude and not to the absolute morphogen levels.
source: In the case of linear decay, the shift is only related to the relative morphogen influx or amplitude and not to the absolute morphogen levels (Appendix 1, Equation 11).
evidence: This is derived from mathematical analysis presented in Appendix 1.

claim: With non-linear decay, the shift depends on the absolute levels, with higher influxes resulting in smaller shifts.
source: However, with non-linear decay, the shift depends on the absolute levels, with higher influxes resulting in smaller shifts (Appendix 1, Equation 12).
evidence: This is derived from mathematical analysis presented in Appendix 1.

claim: Previous research suggested that the circumstance that the shift vanishes for power-law gradients at sufficiently large morphogen influx values leads to more robust patterning.
source: Previous research (Eldar et al., 2003) suggested that the circumstance that this shift vanishes for power-law gradients at sufficiently large morphogen influx values leads to more robust patterning, because the readout position becomes independent of the influx in this limit when the morphogen decay is non-linear (Appendix 1).
evidence: This cites previous theoretical work by Eldar et al., 2003.

claim: Gradients that result from non-linear decay possess significantly shallower tails relative to higher concentration.
source: However, the gradients that result from non-linear decay also possess significantly shallower tails, relative to the higher concentration (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and is a mathematical property of power-law gradients.

claim: The usefulness of non-linear decay gradients for patterning has been questioned.
source: Their usefulness for patterning has therefore been questioned (Lander et al., 2009), and it has remained unclear whether nonlinearity in the morphogen decay would in fact help achieving higher positional accuracy.
evidence: This cites Lander et al., 2009 who questioned the utility of non-linear decay.

claim: To first order, the positional error of variable gradients is inversely proportional to the magnitude of their slope.
source: Indeed, to first order, the positional error of variable gradients is inversely proportional to the magnitude of their slope (Gregor et al., 2007; Vetter and Iber, 2022) according to
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gregor et al., 2007 and Vetter and Iber, 2022.

claim: The positional error of noisy morphogen gradients does not significantly improve with non-linear decay.
source: With this quantitative statistical tool, we demonstrate numerically that the positional error of noisy morphogen gradients does not significantly improve with non-linear decay.
evidence: This is a key finding from the simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: If the morphogen cannot leave the patterned tissue opposite of the source, the power-law gradients become shallow in a substantial part of the domain, leading to reduced positional accuracy with non-linear decay.
source: In the contrary, if the morphogen cannot leave the patterned tissue opposite of the source, the power-law gradients become shallow in a substantial part of the domain, leading to reduced positional accuracy with non-linear decay.
evidence: This is a key finding from the simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The positional error increases with the square root of the cell diameter, irrespective of n.
source: Much as for linear decay (Adelmann et al., 2022), the positional error scales with the square root of the mean cell diameter also for non-linear decay (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and cites previous work.

claim: Small cell diameters are important for high spatial precision also in case of non-linear decay.
source: Small cell diameters, as observed in all known tissues that employ gradient-based patterning (Adelmann et al., 2022), are therefore important for high spatial precision also in case of non-linear decay.
evidence: This is an inference from the scaling relationship shown in Figure 3B and cites Adelmann et al., 2022.

claim: The positional error increases from less than one cell diameter close to the source to about two cell diameters at a distance of 75 cell diameters away from the source.
source: The positional error increases from less than one cell diameter close to the source to about two cell diameters at a distance of 75 cell diameters away from the source (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Close to the distant domain boundary opposite of the source, the positional error rapidly increases for non-linear decay, while remaining relatively low for linear decay.
source: Close to the distant domain boundary opposite of the source, where a no-flux condition was imposed, the positional error rapidly increases for non-linear decay, while remaining relatively low for linear decay.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and is a key finding of the simulations.

claim: The positional error drops in close vicinity to the source with stronger non-linearity in the decay.
source: Independent of whether all parameters are varied or only the production rate, the positional error drops in close vicinity to the source with stronger non-linearity in the decay (insets of Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is shown in the insets of Figures 3C and D.

claim: Further away from the source, linear decay yields a smaller positional error than non-linear decay.
source: Further away from the source, linear decay yields a smaller positional error than non-linear decay (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3D-E.

claim: No matter how long the patterning domain is, non-linearity always increases the positional error as the distal tissue boundary is approached.
source: No matter how long the patterning domain is, non-linearity always increases the positional error as the distal tissue boundary is approached (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Non-linear decay leads to greater positional errors at readout positions in the vicinity of the distal boundary compared to linear decay.
source: By virtue of Equation 5, non-linear decay thus leads to greater positional errors at readout positions in the vicinity of the distal boundary compared to linear decay.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between gradient slope and positional error (Equation 5) and the simulation results.

claim: It is insufficient to quantify gradient robustness and patterning precision by considering variability in the morphogen production alone.
source: In summary, our computer simulations of noisy morphogen gradients suggest that it is insufficient to quantify gradient robustness and patterning precision by considering variability in the morphogen production alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: If the morphogen cannot exit the patterning domain opposite of the source, shifted power-law gradients flatten over a significantly larger range than exponential gradients, leading to increased positional errors.
source: Moreover, if the morphogen cannot exit the patterning domain opposite of the source, shifted power-law gradients that result from non-linear morphogen decay flatten over a significantly larger range than exponential gradients, leading to increased positional errors.
evidence: This is a key finding from the simulations.

claim: The gain in positional accuracy close to the source for non-linear decay is negligible and therefore barely physiologically relevant.
source: The gain in positional accuracy close to the source for non-linear decay is negligible and therefore barely physiologically relevant.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantitative simulation results.

claim: Overall, exponential gradients lead to more robust patterning.
source: Overall, exponential gradients lead to more robust patterning.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the simulation results.

claim: The gradient shapes and positional errors are overall very similar whether the morphogen source is represented by a spatial production domain, by a flux boundary condition, or by a fixed gradient amplitude.
source: While there are small quantitative differences, the gradient shapes (Figure 4A–C) and positional errors (Figure 4D–F) are overall very similar.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4A-F.

claim: Neumann or Dirichlet boundary conditions overestimate the positional error when the variability in the source is high.
source: Neumann or Dirichlet boundary conditions thus overestimate the positional error when the variability in the source is high.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the results in Figures 4D-F.

claim: A spatial source domain should explicitly be modeled, where applicable.
source: Instead of using such boundary conditions, a spatial source domain should explicitly be modeled, where applicable.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the comparison of different modeling approaches.

claim: Molecular noise in morphogen degradation and diffusivity dominates the patterning precision.
source: Molecular noise in morphogen degradation and diffusivity dominates the patterning precision.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results comparing different sources of variability.

claim: The average morphogen production rate is expected to affect the patterning accuracy in the case of non-linear decay, but not for linear decay.
source: As the gradient amplitude determines the sensitivity of the readout position to amplitude changes for non-linear decay (Appendix 1, Equation 12) but not for linear decay (Appendix 1, Equation 11), the average morphogen production rate is expected to affect the patterning accuracy in the case of non-linear decay, but not for linear decay.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on mathematical analysis in Appendix 1.

claim: Changes in morphogen production parameters have no effect on the positional error if morphogen degradation is linear.
source: Changes in these parameters have no effect on the positional error if morphogen degradation is linear, which is consistent with the theory (Figure 5A–F, blue lines).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5A-F and is consistent with theoretical predictions.

claim: With non-linear decay, the positional error is highly dependent on morphogen abundance.
source: With non-linear decay, on the other hand, we indeed observe the positional error to be highly dependent on morphogen abundance.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: Precision arguments previously brought forward for deterministic morphogen gradients do not appear to directly quantitatively translate to the positional error in settings where cell-to-cell variability is included.
source: Precision arguments previously brought forward for deterministic morphogen gradients (Eldar et al., 2003) do not appear to directly quantitatively translate to the positional error in settings where cell-to-cell variability is included, and where morphogen production remains at physiological levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current stochastic results with previous deterministic theory.

claim: For high morphogen supply levels, non-linear decay leads to a smaller positional error close to the source.
source: For high morphogen supply levels, non-linear decay leads to a smaller positional error close to the source (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: The effect of non-linear decay on positional error is substantially less pronounced in the model that includes a spatial morphogen source domain than in those that do not.
source: The effect is, however, substantially less pronounced in the model that includes a spatial morphogen source domain (Figure 5A) than in those that do not (Figure 5B and C), highlighting once again the limitations of the latter.
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figures 5A with 5B and 5C.

claim: The gradients effectively flatten out at low production, reducing their usefulness for spatial tissue patterning.
source: The gradients effectively flatten out at low production, reducing their usefulness for spatial tissue patterning.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results showing increased positional error at low production.

claim: The stronger the non-linearity in the degradation, the more pronounced the loss of patterning precision at low production.
source: The stronger the non-linearity in the degradation, the more pronounced this loss of patterning precision.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Further away from the source, the benefit of non-linear decay is lost entirely, and exponential gradients remain more precise than shifted power-law gradients also at high morphogen supply levels.
source: Further away from the source, the benefit of non-linear decay is lost entirely, and exponential gradients remain more precise than shifted power-law gradients also at high morphogen supply levels (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5D-F.

claim: Simplified models without explicit representation of morphogen-secreting cells overestimate the beneficial impact of non-linear decay on patterning precision.
source: In summary, simplified models without explicit representation of morphogen-secreting cells overestimate the beneficial impact of non-linear decay on patterning precision.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the different modeling approaches in Figure 5.

claim: The benefit of non-linear morphogen decay is restricted to a close vicinity of the morphogen source, where patterning precision is high anyway, and to a regime of very strong morphogen production.
source: In all models considered here, the benefit of non-linear morphogen decay is restricted to a close vicinity of the morphogen source, where patterning precision is high anyway (Vetter and Iber, 2022) and may thus not be as critical for robust development, and to a regime of very strong morphogen production.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results and cites Vetter and Iber, 2022.

claim: Further into the tissue, and at moderate morphogen abundance, linear decay yields more accurate patterning.
source: Further into the tissue, and at moderate morphogen abundance, linear decay yields more accurate patterning.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: While a small advantageous effect of non-linear decay exists near the morphogen source, this gain is outweighed by a substantial loss of precision in the interior and distal parts of a patterned tissue.
source: The surprising outcome of our quantitative analysis is that, while a small advantageous effect indeed exists near the morphogen source, this gain is outweighed by a substantial loss of precision in the spatial information that signalling gradients provide to cells in the interior and distal parts of a patterned tissue when morphogen decay is non-linear.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the quantitative analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In tissues that pose a diffusion barrier to the signalling molecule at their boundary, shifted power-law gradients flatten out over a substantial portion of the spatial domain, whereas exponential gradients remain more graded.
source: In tissues that pose a diffusion barrier to the signalling molecule at their boundary, shifted power-law gradients that emerge with self-enhanced degradation, flatten out over a substantial portion of the spatial domain, whereas exponential gradients remain more graded (Figure 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and is a key finding of the study.

claim: The flattening of power-law gradients leads to greater spatial precision with linear decay.
source: This leads to greater spatial precision with linear decay (Figure 3), and is contrary to the original expectation (Eldar et al., 2003).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and contradicts previous theoretical predictions.

claim: The positional error is highly sensitive to morphogen supply levels when morphogen decay is non-linear, but largely insensitive when decay is linear.
source: The positional error, which is the decisive quantity that measures the spatial accuracy with which cells can determine their location in the pattern, and ultimately their fate in differentiation, is highly sensitive to morphogen supply levels when morphogen decay is non-linear, but largely insensitive when decay is linear (Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: Patterning is more robust to variations in the size and strength of the morphogen-secreting source if decay is linear.
source: This implies that patterning is more robust to variations in the size and strength of the morphogen-secreting source, if decay is linear.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that positional error is insensitive to morphogen supply with linear decay.

claim: The results challenge the established view that power-law gradients buffer fluctuations in morphogen production.
source: These results challenge the established view that power-law gradients buffer fluctuations in morphogen production (Eldar et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a conclusion that contradicts previous theoretical work cited.

claim: The positional error buffers production fluctuations only with linear, but not with non-linear decay.
source: We find that the positional error behaves in the opposite way, buffering production fluctuations only with linear, but not with non-linear decay.
evidence: This is a key finding from the simulations.

claim: A stochastic approach is required to quantify patterning precision of real noisy gradients.
source: Our study demonstrates that a stochastic approach is required to quantify patterning precision of real noisy gradients.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion from the study.

claim: The positional error is overestimated in simplified models that replace the morphogen-secreting cells by a Neumann or Dirichlet boundary condition.
source: Moreover, we find the positional error to be overestimated in simplified models that replace the morphogen-secreting cells by a Neumann or Dirichlet boundary condition (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: An explicit representation of the source should be included in future theoretical or numerical work on the subject.
source: Based on this, we recommend to include an explicit representation of the source in future theoretical or numerical work on the subject, as we did with Equation 6.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Distinguishing exponential gradients from shifted power laws can be very difficult in practice.
source: Distinguishing exponential gradients from shifted power laws can be very difficult in practice, as they can appear similar over the short distances over which they can be reliably measured with classical imaging techniques.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental limitations based on knowledge of measurement techniques.

claim: Most further reports of morphogen gradient shapes are consistent with exponentials within measurement accuracy.
source: Most further reports of morphogen gradient shapes (Gregor et al., 2007; Gregor et al., 2008; Kicheva et al., 2007; Wartlick et al., 2011; Wartlick et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2015; Zagorski et al., 2017; Mateus et al., 2020) are consistent with exponentials within measurement accuracy.
evidence: This cites multiple experimental studies.

claim: New measurement techniques are needed to determine whether non-linear decay is at work in the formation of known morphogen gradients during development.
source: New measurement techniques are needed to determine whether non-linear decay is at work in the formation of known morphogen gradients during development.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the limitations of current measurement techniques.

claim: The data suggest an overall advantage of linear decay, also considering the evolutionary aspect of tissue size and protein synthesis rate differences between species.
source: If anything, our data suggest an overall advantage of linear decay, also considering the evolutionary aspect of tissue size and protein synthesis rate differences between species.
evidence: This is a conclusion and speculation based on the simulation results.

claim: The morphogen concentration declines significantly over several orders of magnitude, independent of whether there is linear or non-linear decay.
source: The morphogen concentration declines significantly over several orders of magnitude, independent of whether there is linear or non-linear decay.
evidence: This is shown in the figures and is a property of both types of gradients.

claim: At low morphogen concentrations, thermal fluctuations and stochastic binding kinetics of ligands and receptors will affect gradient and readout precision.
source: At low morphogen concentrations, thermal fluctuations and stochastic binding kinetics of ligands and receptors will affect gradient and readout precision (Berg and Purcell, 1977; Lauffenburger and Linderman, 1996; Lander et al., 2009).
evidence: This cites theoretical work on molecular fluctuations.

claim: Cells can, in principle, achieve high readout precision despite fluctuations via spatial and temporal averaging.
source: Cells can, in principle, achieve high readout precision despite such fluctuations via spatial and temporal averaging (Lauffenburger and Linderman, 1996).
evidence: This cites theoretical work on cellular averaging mechanisms.

claim: Quantitative measurements of morphogen numbers and cellular responses would be required far away from the source to assess effects of low concentration fluctuations.
source: To assess such effects, quantitative measurements of morphogen numbers and cellular responses would be required far away from the source.
evidence: This is a statement about what would be needed for future experimental work.

claim: More sensitive measurement technology needs to be developed to measure morphogen concentrations far from the source.
source: This requires the further development of more sensitive measurement technology (Lelek et al., 2021).
evidence: This cites work on measurement technology and identifies a need for future development.

claim: Once absolute concentration levels can be determined, it can be assessed whether the approximation of gradients by continuous functions is valid along the whole tissue.
source: Once the absolute concentration levels of the morphogen gradients can be determined, it can be assessed whether the approximation of the gradients by a continuous functions is valid along the whole tissue or, whether discrete models have to be considered.
evidence: This is a statement about future work that would be enabled by better measurements.

claim: Downstream networks would not alter the relative precision of gradients generated by linear and non-linear decay.
source: In future work, the simulated gradients can be used as inputs to complex downstream networks, and the effect of noise in the readout can be studied. However, these downstream networks would not alter the relative precision of gradients generated by linear and non-linear decay.
evidence: This is a speculation about future work and its expected outcomes.

claim: Non-linear decay may slightly enhance precision close to the source, but it rapidly deteriorates far from the source.
source: In conclusion, non-linear decay may slightly enhance precision close to the source, but it rapidly deteriorates far from the source.
evidence: This is the final conclusion summarizing the main findings of the study.

claim: Zero-flux boundary conditions were used at both outer ends of the tissue, mimicking a situation in which morphogen molecules are restricted to the patterned tissue by an impermeable boundary.
source: Zero-flux boundary conditions were used at both outer ends of the tissue, mimicking a situation in which morphogen molecules are restricted to the patterned tissue by an impermeable boundary:
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the computational model.

claim: The readout mechanism has little impact on the gradient precision perceived by the cells.
source: In a recent study, we found that the readout mechanism has little impact on the gradient precision perceived by the cells (Adelmann et al., 2022).
evidence: This cites previous work by the authors.
